question: Explain the doctrine of judicial review in India. How has the Supreme Court used the basic structure doctrine to balance Parliament's amending power and constitutional supremacy?
why: Judicial review is asked 9 times over 7 sittings and constitutional amendments 4 times. The Basic Structure case-law chain is the standard high-scoring structure.
intro: Judicial review is the power of courts to examine the validity of laws and executive actions against the Constitution. In India it is derived from Articles 13, 32, 131, 136, 226 and 227 and is itself part of the basic structure.

pts: Article 13: laws inconsistent with fundamental rights are void; Articles 32 and 226 give writ jurisdiction.
Review of legislative action (competence and rights), executive action (arbitrariness, Article 14) and constitutional amendments.
Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965): Parliament may amend any part.
Golak Nath (1967): Fundamental Rights cannot be amended.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Parliament may amend but not destroy the basic structure.
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), Minerva Mills (1980): limited amending power and judicial review as basic features; Waman Rao and S.R. Bommai (1994): federalism and secularism.
I.R. Coelho (2007): laws in the Ninth Schedule are open to review; NJAC case (2015) struck down the NJAC Act and the 99th Amendment.
Judicial overreach versus restraint; vagueness of what makes the basic structure; pendency of cases.
Need for balance with separation of powers and parliamentary sovereignty.

conclusion: The basic structure doctrine keeps the Constitution's core safe from temporary majorities. Judicial review works best when courts act with restraint and give reasoned judgments.

question: Discuss the emergency provisions of the Indian Constitution and the safeguards introduced after the Emergency of 1975.
why: Emergency provisions (5.2) were asked 3 times and are in the syllabus explicitly. The 44th Amendment safeguards are the usual scoring points.
intro: Part XVIII (Articles 352–360) provides for national, state (President's Rule) and financial emergencies. The Emergency of 1975–77 revealed the risk of misuse and led to changes.

pts: National emergency (Article 352): war, external aggression or armed rebellion (after the 44th Amendment replaced 'internal disturbance').
State emergency (Article 356): failure of constitutional machinery; financial emergency (Article 360), never used so far.

Centre assumes wide legislative and executive control; Article 19 freedoms suspended on war/aggression grounds; Article 359 can suspend enforcement of rights except Articles 20 and 21 after the 44th Amendment.
Written advice of the Union Cabinet needed; parliamentary approval within one month by a special majority; renewal every six months.
Lok Sabha can revoke by simple majority; President's Rule limited and subject to judicial review (S.R. Bommai 1994).
Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions recommended using Article 356 as a last resort.

conclusion: Emergency powers are meant for protecting the Constitution, not for suppressing dissent. Judicial review and parliamentary safeguards have reduced the scope of misuse.

question: The office of the Governor has often been a source of Centre–State friction. Discuss the constitutional position of the Governor and the reforms suggested by various commissions.
why: Role of the Governor is a named syllabus item and federal-structure questions recur (2.1 asked 8 times). Commission recommendations are standard material.
intro: The Governor is the constitutional head of the state and also the Centre's representative. This dual role has led to controversies over appointment of Chief Ministers, dissolution of assemblies, reservation of Bills and delay in assent.

pts: Articles 153–167: appointed by the President, holds office during pleasure, acts on the advice of the council of ministers except in discretionary matters.
Powers: summoning and proroguing the legislature, assent or reservation of Bills (Article 200), ordinances (Article 213), reports for Article 356 and discretion in a hung assembly.
Partisan appointments of political persons; arbitrary removal; delay on assent; misuse of Article 356 (Rameshwar Prasad 2006, Bommai 1994).
Sarkaria (1988): non-partisan eminent person, not active in politics recently, consultation with the Chief Minister.
Punchhi (2010): fixed tenure and removal by impeachment-like process; Venkatachaliah Commission.
Supreme Court rulings on timelines for assent to Bills and the scope of discretion.

conclusion: The Governor should act as a bridge, not a political agent. Clear conventions on discretion and fixed tenure will build trust in cooperative federalism.

theme: RTI, Citizen's Charter, social audit and good governance
question: Right to Information, Citizen's Charters and social audit are tools of transparency and accountability. Evaluate their effectiveness in Indian governance.
why: Good governance topics (10.x) appear in the 2026 syllabus including Public Service Act and social audit; RTI has been asked 3 times. A tools-and-effectiveness combo is a probable form.
intro: Good governance rests on transparency, accountability and responsiveness. India has introduced the RTI Act (2005), Citizen's Charters (1997 onward) and social audit (MGNREGS) to hold administration to account.

pts: RTI Act 2005: request for information within 30 days, Central and State Information Commissions, proactive disclosure (Section 4).
Citizen's Charter: public commitments on service standards, time limits and grievance redress; Sevottam model.
Social audit: community verification of records, mandated under MGNREGA; Meghalaya and Andhra Pradesh social audit units as examples.
Exposed corruption (Adarsh, 2G) and improved access to rations, pensions and wages; millions of RTI applications each year.
Limits: backlog in Information Commissions, vacancies, attacks on RTI users, dilution through the DPDP Act's amendment of Section 8(1)(j), charters that are not enforceable.
Statutory Citizen's Charter and Public Service Guarantee Act, e-governance dashboards, protection of whistle-blowers, staffing of commissions.

conclusion: These tools move governance from secrecy to answerability. Their effectiveness depends on enforcement and citizens' awareness.

theme: Ethics, integrity and accountability in public service
question: What do you understand by integrity and accountability in public service? Discuss the ethical dilemmas faced by civil servants and how codes of conduct and Lokpal/Lokayukta help.
why: Ethics in Public Service (Section C) is asked 1–2 times a sitting. Defining concepts and linking them to institutions is the standard structure.
intro: Integrity means consistency between values, words and actions, even when unobserved. Accountability means answering for one's decisions to the people and the law. Together they form the ethical basis of public service.

pts: Seven Nolan principles: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership.
Constitutional morality, impartiality, empathy, dedication to public service.
Political pressure versus rule of law; confidentiality versus transparency; loyalty to superiors versus public interest; personal beliefs versus duty.
Conduct Rules, Prevention of Corruption Act (2018 amendment), Central Vigilance Commission, Lokpal and Lokayukta, whistle-blower protection, RTI and Citizen's Charters.
Training, ethical leadership and culture; examples such as T.N. Seshan and E. Sreedharan.

conclusion: Rules can punish wrongdoing, but values prevent it. An administration with integrity at every level builds citizens' trust in democracy.

theme: Basic knowledge of laws: cyber laws, GST, labour laws, criminal law
question: Explain the main features of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam. How do they change the criminal justice system?
why: The 2026 syllabus has a new 'Basic knowledge of laws in India' block (criminal laws, labour, cyber and tax). The three new criminal codes are the obvious factual question.
intro: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) came into force on 1 July 2024 replacing the Indian Penal Code 1860, the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 and the Indian Evidence Act 1872.

pts: BNS: new offences such as organised crime, terrorism, mob lynching and snatching; community service as a punishment; sedition replaced by a provision on acts endangering sovereignty; gender-neutral language in some offences.
BNSS: time limits for investigation and trial, mandatory forensic visits for serious crimes, e-FIR and zero FIR, audio-video recording of searches, trial in absentia.
BSA: electronic and digital records treated as primary evidence; admissibility of electronic evidence with certification.
Faster justice and modern evidence; improved victim focus.
Concerns: longer police custody provisions, wide powers, preparedness of courts and police training, and need for infrastructure.

conclusion: The new codes modernise a colonial framework. Their success will depend on capacity building, safeguards for rights and consistent judicial interpretation.
updates: Check any Supreme Court or High Court rulings on BNS/BNSS provisions and the latest amendments
